title: The loon
hookLine: he chased a loon on the pond that laughed and dived (Walden 12)

cards: A calm afternoon in fall. The pond is flat as glass. Thoreau is out in his boat, and not far off sits a loon, a big black-and-white diving bird.
He paddles toward it. It dives. He stops, scanning the water, guessing where it will come up.
It surfaces somewhere else entirely, far off, sometimes behind him. And then it laughs, that long, wild call rolling across the water. So he picks a new direction and tries again.

teach.b: First, the game. In Brute Neighbors, Thoreau tells the chase move by move, and calls it what it is: "a pretty game, played on the smooth surface of the pond, a man against a loon." Notice the word game.
He isn't hunting it or trying to hurt it. He wants to outguess it, and he keeps losing. Second, the cleverness.

teach.h: IT COMES UP WHERE YOU DON'T LOOK.
teach.b: The loon picks the widest stretch of water to dive in, stays down long, swims far underneath, and comes up where he least expected. This is the man who sounded the whole pond with a line and stone.
He knows this water, and a bird still runs rings around him. Third, the laughter. Each time it comes up, it calls, and Thoreau hears the call as a laugh, wild and unearthly.
He wonders if the bird is laughing at him. He doesn't sound offended. He sounds delighted.
Fourth, the ending. The wind rises, a light rain begins, and Thoreau half-jokes that it's as if the loon had called on its god for help, and the god had answered.
He gives up, and the loon is left out on the water, unbeaten. There's a kind of freedom in that ending. Not everything has to be caught, solved or won.
Some things are better for being wilder than you are, and the best you can do is enjoy the game.

how: Readers of Brute Neighbors often enjoy the loon chase as a picture of meeting something wild with play rather than control, and of taking defeat with good humor.

games.why: the wind and rain came, he gave up, and the loon stayed unbeaten. he tells it as a game he enjoyed losing.

practice: Bring to mind something you can't control or predict, the weather, a cat, a small child, your own wandering mind, and let it be the loon: watch it dive and come up somewhere else, and notice the urge to chase it down.
For this one sit, let it win. If your attention wanders, don't drag it back hard; smile at where it surfaced, and come back gently.
